verses.text: The first book I wrote, Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began both to do and to teach,
until the day in which he was received up, after he had given commandment through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
To these he also showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days, and speaking about God’s Kingdom.
Being assembled together with them, he commanded them, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me.
For John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”
Therefore when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?”
He said to them, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”
When he had said these things, as they were looking, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight.
While they were looking steadfastly into the sky as he went, behold,  two men stood by them in white clothing,
who also said, “You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.”
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.

When they had come in, they went up into the upper room, where they were staying; that is Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James.
All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.
In these days, Peter stood up in the middle of the disciples (and the number of names was about one hundred twenty), and said,
“Brothers, it was necessary that this Scripture should be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke before by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who was guide to those who took Jesus.
For he was counted with us, and received his portion in this ministry.
Now this man obtained a field with the reward for his wickedness, and falling headlong, his body burst open, and all his intestines gushed out.
It became known to everyone who lived in Jerusalem that in their language that field was called ‘Akeldama,’ that is, ‘The field of blood.’
For it is written in the book of Psalms, ‘Let his habitation be made desolate. Let no one dwell therein;’   and, ‘Let another take his office.’
“Of the men therefore who have accompanied us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,
beginning from the baptism of John, to the day that he was received up from us, of these one must become a witness with us of his resurrection.”
They put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
They prayed, and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen
to take part in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas fell away, that he might go to his own place.”
They drew lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles.

footnotes.content: Luke says he's already written his gospel—now he's continuing the story. What Jesus *began* to do, His work goes on through His followers. That word 'began' stays with me: the resurrection wasn't an ending, but the true beginning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The apostles received their orders—not in chaos after the crucifixion, but given carefully by the risen Jesus, through the Holy Spirit. Even in our confusion, the Lord is speaking clear instruction to those who've chosen to follow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty days of proof. Jesus appeared again and again, not as a ghost or a distant memory, but alive—eating, talking, real enough to touch. The kingdom He taught about wasn't cancelled; it was restarted in their hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gathered together, Jesus commands them to wait. Not to go out yet, not to act yet. How hard that must have been—they'd seen Him alive, seen the evidence, felt the fire—and now they had to wait. Obedience often wears the face of patience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Water baptism marked the old way; now comes a baptism in the Spirit—a changed heart, not just a changed appearance. John baptized the outside; the Holy Spirit baptizes the inside. Soon, not many days hence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even now, standing with the risen Jesus, they ask about restoring the kingdom to Israel. How human—we frame the Lord's work in our own hopes. They want the kingdom back. He wants something far deeper: the kingdom *inside* every heart that believes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesus won't tell them when. The times and seasons belong to the Father alone, hidden in His authority. What a mercy—we're freed from that burden of knowing. We're called only to be faithful now, in this moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Power comes first—the Holy Spirit, not their strength or cleverness. Then their calling: to witness, not to argue or persuade, just to tell what they've seen. And the reach: from home, to neighbors, to the ends of the earth. Every believer carries this same commission.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Ascension—He goes up, a cloud takes Him, and they lose sight. Not abandonment, but a new kind of presence. He leaves them not orphaned but sent. The physical departure opens the spiritual sending.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They stand staring into the sky—I can picture it, the apostles frozen in wonder, watching Him vanish. Then two figures in white appear. The sudden arrival of heaven's messengers often interrupts our gaze upward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angels gently rebuke: why are you standing here looking up? Jesus will return the same way He left—visible, real, in the sky. But that's not today's work. Today belongs to witness and waiting, not gazing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the Mount of Olives—the same mountain where Jesus wept over Jerusalem, where He was betrayed, where He faced the cost of our salvation. Now from that place of sorrow, the apostles return to the city with hope and a promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An upper room, and ten names listed—Peter, John, James, and the others. Notice who's missing: Judas. The apostolic band is broken but not abandoned; they gather in the same place where Jesus taught them, waiting and faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One accord, steadfast prayer—and the women are there, and Mary, Jesus's mother. Not sidelined, but gathered, praying with the apostles. His brothers, too, who didn't believe in Him during His ministry, now stand with the company of believers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: About a hundred twenty souls—not just the Twelve, but a small congregation. Peter stands and speaks, already showing the courage the Lord promised. From the man who denied Jesus to the voice calling the flock to faithfulness: a miracle in itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter points to Scripture about Judas, seeing God's hand at work even in betrayal. The Holy Spirit spoke it through David long ago. God's Word held the whole story—even the stumbling, even the fall—before it happened.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judas was counted with them, had his share in the ministry. He wasn't an outsider picked for destruction; he walked with Jesus, saw the miracles, received the calling. His fall comes from intimacy broken, not from distance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plain truth: Judas fell and died—money bought him in, but money couldn't save him. The text spares no one's feelings about his end. Greed's wages come due, and the cost is always higher than we reckoned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Akeldama, the field of blood. A place name carved into history by sorrow. But notice: Jerusalem *knew* about it, talked about it, named it. Public shame, yet the gospel still moved forward. Failure doesn't stop the Lord's purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Scripture says his dwelling will be desolate, another will take his place. Peter quotes the Psalms to make sense of betrayal through God's Word. When our hearts are broken, the Bible can be our steadying hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Only someone who was *there*—who lived through it all with Jesus, from start to finish—could fill this role. Not a latecomer, not someone with secondhand faith, but a witness to the whole story. Some tasks require the whole journey.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From John's baptism to the resurrection—one of these men had walked the entire road with Jesus. To be a witness of the resurrection, you had to know Him before it, and after. Full knowledge, full faith, full commitment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias—two faithful men, either could have served. Both had walked the way, both deserved consideration. Sometimes the Lord asks us to choose among good options, not between good and evil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The apostles pray directly to the Lord Jesus: You know all hearts, show us which one. Not a power grab, but a plea for discernment. They appeal to His knowledge, not their own judgment. This is how the early church decided.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judas fell away from his place. Not erased from history—he's remembered, talked about, his office still speaking—but he lost his standing. Every calling carries the freedom to refuse it. That freedom cuts both ways.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cast lots, and Matthias becomes the twelfth. Readers today hear an echo of the Lord still choosing—not through lots anymore, but through the Spirit. Yet the principle holds: the Lord fills empty places with faithful hearts. We, too, wait on His choosing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
